result:
**Last Times**

We keep careful track of first times. First word, first step, first tooth under the pillow, first day of school with the too-big backpack and the photograph taken against the front door. Whole industries exist to help us record them. There is a page in the baby book for the first haircut and a little envelope, sometimes, to hold the hair.

There is no page for last times. Nobody hands you a form to fill out on the last night you carry your child up the stairs to bed. You do it the way you did it four hundred times before — the weight shifted onto your hip, the head heavy against your collarbone, the negotiation at the top of the landing about whether the hall light stays on — and then you don't do it again, and no one announces this, and the not-doing spreads out silently over the following years like water finding a floor.

I think about the last game of a childhood. Somewhere there was an afternoon when the neighborhood kids played whatever they played, kickball or ghost in the graveyard or the elaborate serial dramas that get invented under a particular tree, and someone's mother called them in for dinner, and that was the end of it. Not the end of that game. The end of games. Nobody knew. They went in and ate and the next day it rained, or somebody got a new thing to be interested in, or the season shifted a degree and the light was wrong, and it simply never resumed. The whole apparatus — the rules refined over months, the tree, the roles, the ferocity of it — dissolved without ceremony. The children who dissolved it are now adults who can't tell you when it happened.

This should be unbearable and mostly it isn't, and I've been trying to understand why.

Part of it is that we are not built to hold that much attention. If I knew that this was the last time I would drink coffee from this particular chipped mug — that tomorrow it goes into the sink and out of the sink into the box and out of the box into a stranger's kitchen — I would have to feel something about it, and I would be feeling something about approximately nine hundred objects and gestures per day, and I would get nothing done. The ignorance is load-bearing. It's not a flaw in the design; it's the reason the design can move.

But I don't think that's all of it. I think we also want the ordinary to be ordinary. There's a particular grace available only to things you do without knowing they matter. The last time my grandmother told me a story about her sister, she wasn't performing a last story. She was just talking, and interrupting herself, and getting the year wrong and correcting it, and stopping to check whether the kettle had boiled. If she had known, it would have become a different kind of object — polished, aware of itself, a monument instead of a Tuesday. I have the Tuesday. I think the Tuesday is better, though I would trade almost anything for one more of them.

Still. There's a thing worth practicing, which is not knowing but suspecting.

Not the grim version — not walking around murmuring *memento mori* at the breakfast table, which is its own kind of failure to be present, a way of tasting your own profundity instead of the toast. Something lighter. A habit of occasionally noticing: this is a *time*. Not the last, probably, but a member of a finite set. There are only so many of these. The set has an edge somewhere out ahead of me in the fog.

The number of times I will see a certain friend is a number. It's not a large number. If we manage twice a year and we're both lucky about our health, it's maybe sixty more evenings, total, which sounds like a lot until you notice that sixty evenings is two months of evenings, which is to say: I have two months left with this person, distributed thinly across three decades. That reframe is either horrifying or clarifying depending on the day and, I suspect, on whether you do anything with it.

What you do with it, I think, is small. You stay for one more drink. You pick up the phone instead of texting, occasionally, on purpose. You let the child stay up. You take the long way home when the light does the thing it does in October. You don't try to make the moment significant, because you can't, significance isn't a thing you can install — but you can decline to hurry, which is nearly the same and much more achievable.

And you forgive yourself for the ones you missed, because you missed almost all of them. That's the arithmetic. Every day is composed largely of last times you failed to salute. The last time you'll ever hear a particular song by accident in a store. The last time you park in this spot. The last conversation with someone who moves away and whom you fully intend to keep up with. Grief, at least a certain low-grade ambient kind of it, is just the accumulated residue of ordinary continuance. Everyone is carrying it. Almost no one mentions it.

There's a counterweight, too, and it's the same fact from the other side: you also don't know when you're doing something for the *first* time in a way that will matter. The book you pick up in the waiting room. The person who sits down next to you because there's nowhere else. The offhand remark that turns out to be the hinge. Most first times are as unmarked as most last times. The baby book is a lie of retrospect; we only know which firsts were firsts because we later stopped counting.

So the fog cuts both ways, and this is either terrible or, on a good day, the most hopeful thing available. Somewhere in the ordinary undifferentiated middle of this week there is something beginning that I won't recognize for years.

I'd like to be paying attention when it happens. I won't be. That's fine.

I'll notice later, and be grateful, and get the year wrong when I tell it.

I'm drawn to the idea of writing about the last time we do things without knowing it's the last time—when your child stops asking to be carried, when you play outside as a kid for the final time. That's real, moving material with genuine philosophical weight. I'll write it with texture and specificity rather than sentimentality, maybe ending without a neat resolution, letting the mercy of not knowing sit there.
